study.title: Ecclesiastes 6 - Wealths without the ability to enjoy, long life without satisfaction and human limitation before the future
study.overview: This chapter denounces one of the great ironies of life under the sun: one can receive wealth, honor, children and long life, but not receive from God the ability to enjoy what he possesses. The text shows that material abundance does not guarantee joy, security or sense. It also insists that human desires are restless, that excessive speech does not solve the futility of existence and that the human being dominates neither the present nor the future. The conclusion is sober: as life is brief and transient, practical wisdom is in accepting human limits and living with realism before God.

outline.title: A well received but not enjoyed
outline.explanation: The openness presents a frequent evil: a person receives wealth, possessions and honor, but God does not grant him the ability to enjoy them. The stranger ends up consuming the fruit of work, and this is described as vanity and suffering. The problem is not only to possess, but to have without joy.

outline.title: Long life, children and honor are not enough
outline.explanation: The text uses a strong comparison: even with many children and many years, without contentment and without a worthy end, life may be worse than not being born. The image of lifeless birth and denied burial emphasizes that longevity and fertility do not compensate for an empty existence.

outline.title: Human appetite never satisfies
outline.explanation: Human work tends to maintain the body, but does not fill the soul. The wise and fool, the rich and the poor, face the same basic limitation: restless desire, greed without rest and few real advantages. The multiplication of words also does not solve futility; rather, it can increase it. Man cannot contend with someone more powerful than him.

outline.title: The inability to know what is best and what will come
outline.explanation: The closure summarizes the tone of the chapter: no one knows, for itself, what is really good in this passing life, nor can it say what will happen after his death. Existence is short as shadow, and the future remains out of human reach.

study.context: The chapter continues the sapienciaI reflection of Ecclesiastes on the life underneath the sun', that is, the human experience observed in the common order of this world. The text does not present here a political or economic solution, but a criticism of the illusion that goods, status and long-lasting guarantee well-being. The background is the observation of real life: there are people who accumulate, but do not enjoy; they speak much, but they do not advance; they plan the future, but do not control it.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter emphasizes God's sovereignty over possession and pleasure. It is not enough for the human being to receive goods; it is God who also grants, or denies, the ability to take advantage of them. This confronts human autonomy and dismantles the idea that happiness is a simple product of accumulation. The text also reveals the fragility of the human condition: insatiable desires, inevitable death, limited language and ignorance of the future. In evangelical reading, this points to the need for humility, gratitude and dependence on God, rather than trust in riches or self-control. At the same time, criticism of futility is not an invitation to despair, but to practical wisdom: to receive God's gifts with fear, contentment and discernment.

scholarViews.insight: Man can have everything and yet still fails to enjoy; the gain without the ability to enjoyment continues to be tragedy and vanity.
Wealths, children and long life do not compensate for an existence without contentment; outer honor loses value when a worthy end and a service life is lacking.
Human work keeps the mouth, but does not satisfy the soul; therefore, even continuous effort does not resolve inner dissatisfaction.

questions: In which areas do you run the risk of confusing possession with contentment, as if you have the same as enjoying?
What does the text reveal about the difference between a long life and a truly meaningful life before God?
How does your speech, your plans and your concerns show confidence in self-control, rather than humility before God's sovereignty?
study.practice: Practice an honest assessment of your possessions, designs and desires: thank God for what you have received, ask Him for the ability to enjoy with gratitude and give up the illusion that more things will solve the restlessness of the soul. Today, choose a concrete attitude of contentment, generosity and sobriety - for example, using a resource that you usually accumulate to bless someone, rather than just keep for yourself. It also limits unnecessary words and give to God what you cannot control, including tomorrow.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text presented is in Portuguese and was the main basis of the study; the notes of the commentators were used only as interpretive voices. It is not possible to state with certainty, only from these notes, broader historical details about authorship, date or specific circumstances of the composition. In 6:10, Tyndale's note makes an interpretive connection with other biblical passages over divine sovereignty, but this does not define the full meaning of the verse alone. In verse 12, there are also possible translations for some expressions, and the study seeks to preserve the general meaning without relying on linguistic choices not explained in the notes.
